units.text: Integrating multi-omics data to optimize immunotherapy in endometrial cancer: a comprehensive study
Introduction

Endometrial cancer (EC) is one of the most common gynecological cancers globally.Recent statistics report approximately 42,000 new cases and 97,000 deaths annually, with a projected increase of up to 50-100% in the next decade [1].Postmenopausal bleeding, while not specific to EC, occurs in about 90% of cases and serves as a key early warning sign [2,3].Early diagnosis often enables effective treatment through surgery [3,4].Although traditional therapies-surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy-improve survival, they offer limited benefit for patients with advanced or recurrent disease [2,[5][6][7].

In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising alternative for treating various cancers, including EC.Instead of attacking tumor cells directly, immunotherapy strengthens the body's immune system to recognize and destroy cancer cells [8][9][10].Immune checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and dostarlimab, which target PD-1/PD-L1 pathways, have been approved for EC treatment by the FDA.These drugs have shown improved outcomes in patients who are resistant to conventional therapy [11,12].However, many patients do not respond to immunotherapy, and the reasons for this variability remain unclear [7,11,13,14].

The tumor microenvironment (TME)-a dynamic mix of immune, stromal, and tumor cells-plays a crucial role in modulating treatment outcomes [15,16].Cytotoxic T cells are central to immune defense, but their function can be suppressed by immune checkpoint molecules such as CTLA-4 and PD-L1, often expressed by regulatory T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) [17,18].Other TME components, including tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) [19] natural killer cells (NKs) [20] dendritic cells (DCs) [21] fibroblasts, and endothelial cells (ECs) [18,22] also influence immunotherapy effectiveness.

The advent of high-throughput sequencing technology has furnished researchers with invaluable instruments to facilitate research in the field of cancer, most notably in the domain of immunotherapy for EC patients [23][24][25][26].However, the majority of contemporary studies remain constrained to the implementation of single-omics approaches (e.g.transcriptomics [26]proteomics [25] and genomics [23,24]) or concentrate on specific biological pathways, lacking systematic analysis from a multi-omics perspective.Among the TME of patients in the NR group.These macrophages facilitate angiogenesis and cell proliferation through intercellular communication with subpopulations such as endothelial and epithelial cells.TME of patients in the R group exhibited an enrichment of M1-like TAMs, which primarily engaged with immune cells via diverse immune-activating factors.Furthermore, immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry demonstrated that responders to immunotherapy had significantly increased infiltration of M1-like TAMs.M1-like TAMs were shown to inhibit proliferation and migration of Ishikawa cells in co-culture assays.This research offers a comprehensive insight into the multi-omics level factors influencing the immunotherapy response of EC patients, emphasizing the influence of genomic variants and TAMs on said response.This contributes to an enhanced comprehension of the biological mechanisms underlying EC immunotherapy response and aids in the optimization of EC immunotherapy.

them, various multi-omics integration strategies, including Subtype-GAN [27], iCluF [28], iClusterPlus [29], LRAcluster [30] and CIMLR [31] have been employed in other cancers and have been proven to effectively promote personalized treatment for cancer patients.Consequently, there is a necessity to comprehensively explore the biological pathways related to immunotherapy in EC patients through multi-omics data integration to identify the factors affecting its immunotherapeutic efficacy, thereby promoting personalized treatment.

In this study, we classified EC patients into response (R) and non-response (NR) groups using computational tools and multi-omics data.We examined key differences in gene mutations, biological pathways, and immune cell infiltration between groups.By integrating bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, we further analyzed cellular composition and molecular interactions within the TME.Our findings offer a detailed view of the immune-related factors influencing treatment response in EC and provide a foundation for developing more precise, personalized immunotherapy strategies.
Materials and methods
Data collection and pre-processing

RNA-seq (Counts and TPM value) data, clinicopathological data, somatic mutations, and copy number variation (CNV) data from EC patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database were downloaded using the R package "TCGAbiolinks" [32] (v.2.28.3).Samples were identified, and only data from tumor tissues were retained.

Raw data of microarray was obtained from the NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database under accession number GSE120490 [33].The R package "oligo" (v.1.64.1) was used for raw data reading and quality control, and "AnnoProbe" (v.0.1.7)performed gene ID transformation of the matrix.The matrix was log-transformed while Gene Symbol that occur repeatedly are retained at their mean value.

The single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from EC patients were downloaded from the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) database under accession number SRP349751 [34].Raw reads in the fastq files were processed in the Cell Ranger Software Suite (10x Genomics Cell Ranger 4.0.0)[35] using refdata-gex-GRCh38-2020-A as reference to map reads on the human genome (GRCh38), and generated the unique molecular identifier (UMI) matrices.The Cell Ranger outputs were imported into Seurat [36] (v.4.3.0.1).Among each sample, cells with UMI counts above upper 10%, fewer than 500 UMI counts or more than 40% mitochondrial UMI counts were filtered out.In addition, genes expressed in less than 10 cells were excluded.After the quality filtering, 21,703 cells from 5 subjects were selected for the following analysis.
This study utilizes data from publicly available databases.Figure 1 depicts the flowchart of this study.
Immunotherapy response

The Tumor Immune Dysfunction and Exclusion (TIDE) score were calculated and the immunotherapy response was accessed using the TIDE algorithm [37] under a Linux system.Based on the TIDE outcomes, the EC patients were classified into two groups, namely non-response (NR) and response (R).Additionally, we utilized the R package "easier" [38]
Functional enrichment analysis

RNA-seq (Counts value) data and microarray data were respectively analyzed using the DEseq2(v.1.40.2) [40] and limma (v.3.56.2) [41].DESeq2 was selected for the analysis of RNA-seq data due to its model-based approach, which is well-suited for handling count data and accounting for variance across biological replicates [40].Limma, on the other hand, was employed for microarray data as it is specifically optimized for differential expression analysis in such datasets, using empirical Bayes methods to improve statistical power [41].The genes with adj.P < 0.05 and |log 2 FC| ≥ 1.5 were defined as differentially expressed genes (DEGs).The sorted Entrez-ID of DEGs was used to support the functional enrichment analysis for Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) in clusterProfiler (v.4.8.2) [42] with the signaling pathways with P < 0.05 considered significant.

Ggvenn (v.0.1.10)was utilized to draw the Venn diagram, which was employed to discern the commonalities and unique characteristics of DEGs across disparate datasets.Furthermore, we conducted a functional enrichment analysis on genes that exhibited consistent differential expression trends in both independent datasets, with the signaling pathways with P < 0.05 considered significant.
Tumor microenvironment analysis

The ESTIMATE [43] algorithm was used to calculate the Stromalscore, Immunescore, ESTIMATEscore, and Tumorpurity in EC patients.The TIMER [44] and EPIC [45] algorithms were utilized to decode the tumor microenvironment (TME) contexture, respectively.ESTIMATE was chosen due to its capacity to estimate stromal and immune cell infiltration levels based on transcriptomic data, providing an overview of the immune and stromal contributions in TME.TIMER, on the other hand, was selected for its ability to assess immune cell composition without being influenced by gene expression levels.It focuses on the correlation between tissue-specific and immune cell-specific genes, correcting for collinearity to mitigate the impact of low expression or collinearity on the results.EPIC, in contrast, uses circulating immune cells or tumor-infiltrating non-malignant cells as references, making it particularly useful for identifying undercharacterized, potentially highly variable cell types.The combination of these three methods was chosen to ensure a more detailed and multi-faceted analysis of the TME, complementing each other by capturing both the overall immune environment and specific immune cell interactions.

The 29 TME gene expression signatures identified by Bagaev et al. [46] which were then extracted and transformed into the gmt files.The 'gsva' function of GSVA [47] was used to perform gene set variation analysis (GSVA).Furthermore, log 2 FC were calculated for two independent datasets, sorted from smallest to largest, and the top 200 and bottom 200 were extracted to construct new gene sets.The 'GSEA' function of cluster-Profiler [42] was utilized to perform gene set enrichment analysis, where P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The list of genes for immune checkpoints, chemokines and receptors, interferons and receptors, and interleukins and receptors were extracted from the published literature [6].Gene expression was then normalized, and P < 0.05 was considered to indicate significant differences in expression between groups.
Somatic mutations analysis

The somatic mutation analysis in this study were all performed by R package "maftools" [48] (v.2.16.0).The 'mafCompare' function was used to identify differentially mutated genes between NR and R, and the top 20 genes were visualized by the 'coOncoplot' function.The 'trinucleotideMatrix' and 'extractSignatures' functions were used to identify retained characteristic mutation patterns in the cancer progression processes, thus enabling the interpretation of mutations as potential mutagenic processes [49].The 'somaticInteractions' function was used to identify pairs of genes mutated in a mutually exclusive or coexisting manner.Furthermore, functional enrichment analysis of the top 20 genes has identified biological pathways that may be affected by their mutations.P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Copy number variation analysis

Download the snp6.na35.remap.hg38.subset.txt.gzfile from GitHub ( h t t p s : / / g i t h u b .c o m / N C I -G D C / d n a c o p y -t o o l / ) as a maker file.Split the masked copy number s e g m e n t according to the grouping of EC patients and use them as the segment file for NR and R respectively.The maker file and segment file were uploaded to the GenePattern (https://www.genepattern.org/)website, while Human_hg38.UCSC.add_mir.160920.mat was selected as the reference file, and finally, the GISTIC 2.0 [50] module was run to investigate the CNVs of R and NR.After the run results are obtained, the R package "BSgenome.Hsapiens.UCSC.hg38"(v.1.4.5) was used to identify the chromosomal location of any amplification or deletion events.In addition, the 'gisticOncoPlot' function of maftools [48] (v.2.16.0) was used to visualize CNV events occurring with a frequency of the top 20 in NR and R.
Dimension reduction and integration of single-cell RNA sequencing data

The Seurat [36] (v.4.3.0.1) functions NormalizeData and ScaleData were used to normalize and scale the preprocessed data, respectively, while FindVariableGenes was used to identify highly variable genes.The "RunPCA" function was used to estimate the principal components (PCs).Then, the dimension range was set to 1:40, and the "RunUMAP" functions were used to perform the Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection downscaling (UMAP).
In order to eliminate the batch effect caused by the difference of sample sources, we used the "harmony" function of R package "harmony" (0.1.1)for data integration.
Unsupervised clustering of single-cell RNA sequencing data

Set reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:40, and use the Seurat [36] (v.4.3.0.1) function Find-Neighbors to allocate cells.In addition, set different resolutions and run FindClusters for unsupervised clustering.In conclusion, we displayed the clustering of cells at various resolutions in a tree format.We then selected the stable outcomes for further analysis.

Followed the guidelines for single-cell transcriptome annotation [51] we collected published classical cell markers and identified seven cell types: lymphocytes (CCL5, STK17B) [34,52] the unciliated epithelium (EPCAM + , CDH1 + , CDHR3 -, FOXJ1 − ) [34,52,53] stromal fibroblasts (DCN, COL6A3) [34,52] the ciliated epithelium (EPCAM + , CDH1 + , CDHR3 + , FOXJ1 + ) 34,52,53 , smooth muscle cells (ACTA2, RGS5) [34,52,54] endothelial cells (PECAM1, PCDH17) [34,52] and macrophages (MS4A6A, CD68) [34,55].In addition, we further validated the accuracy of the annotation by the cell markers identified by Ren et al. [34].
Identifying immunotherapy response-related subpopulations by integrating bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing data

We identified immunotherapy response-related subpopulations by the Scissor algorithm [56].Briefly, we used NR and R as the phenotype for EC patients while collating a scRNA-seq expression matrix and bulk profiling data.The above three files were used as input data for Scissor, where R was defined as a positive outcome and NR as a negative outcome.A regression model was built against the dichotomous variables to calculate the regression coefficients for each cell against the phenotype.Cells with negative regression coefficients are highly correlated with NR, described as "Scissor_NR", cells with positive regression coefficients are highly correlated with R, described as " Scissor_R", and cells with zero regression coefficients are background cells, described as "NULL".
Subpopulation identification, enrichment analysis, feature scoring

Extract macrophages and perform t-distributed stochastic neighborhood embedding (t-SNE) dimensionality reduction using the "RunTSNE" function.Unsupervised clustering was run and the most stable result was selected.Using the Seurat [36] (v.4.3.0.1) function FindMarkers, we identified top 15 genes of each subpopulation.

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) [42] was carried out using the KEGG gene set, where a p value < 0.05 was considered to be a significantly different pathway.In compliance with Sun et al. [57]we used the UCell [58] algorithm to score the cell cycle score, pro-inflammatory score and anti-inflammatory score of the cell populations separately.
Cell-cell interaction analysis

Cell-cell interaction analysis between cell populations was inferred from CellChat [59].By using the default settings, the "computeCommunProbPathway" function was able to create a cellular communication network by summarizing all the ligand-receptor pairs.To determine the number of interactions between two cell populations, the "netVisual_ circle" function was utilized.The "netAnalysis_signalingRole_scatter" function was then used to create a two-dimensional visualization of the primary senders and receivers.Finally, the "netVisual_bubble" function was used to summarize the significant interactions between these two cell populations.
Patient cohorts and tissue collection

A total of 12 EC patients who underwent surgical resection were included in this study at the Department of Gynecology, the Affiliated Dalian Third People's Hospital of Dalian Medical University.All patients had histologically confirmed diagnoses and provided written informed consent prior to surgery.This study was approved by the Affiliated Dalian Third People's Hospital of Dalian Medical University Ethics Committee (2024-185-001).Patients received 2-4 cycles of neoadjuvant immunotherapy.Among these, 6 patients exhibited non-major pathological responses postoperatively, while 6 patients demonstrated major pathological responses (residual viable tumor in the primary tumor and lymph nodes ≤ 10%) or complete pathological remission (residual viable tumor in the primary tumor and lymph nodes = 0%).Patients were categorized as non-response (NR) (n = 6) and response (R) (n = 6), respectively.In all cases, fresh tumor tissue and peripheral blood were collected immediately for tissue processing.
Immunohistochemistry

Tissue section (4 µm) were prepared and subjected to deparaffinization and rehydration using a series of ethanol solutions.Antigen retrieval was achieved through heatinduced methods.To block endogenous peroxidase activity, sections were treated with 3% hydrogen peroxide for 15 min.Primary antibodies, CD86 (28058-1-AP, Proteintech, Wuhan, China) and CD206 (60143-1-Ig, Proteintech, Wuhan, China), were applied and incubated overnight at 4 °C.After washing with PBS, sections were incubated with a secondary HRP-conjugated antibody (SP-9000, Zsbio, Beijing, China) for 20 min at room temperature.Visualization was performed using 3,3'-diaminobenzidine (DAB, AR1021, Boster, Wuhan, China), and the slides were counterstained with hematoxylin.After dehydration and clearing, the sections were mounted and scanned using a whole-slide imaging system (SQS-40R, Shengqiang, Shenzhen, China).
Flow cytometry

Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from the peripheral blood of endometrial cancer (EC) patients using Ficoll density gradient centrifugation.The isolated cells were cryopreserved in CellBanker 1® medium (Takara Bio Inc., Tokyo, Japan) at − 80 °C.Frozen PBMCs were thawed, suspended in 50 µL of PBS, and incubated for 30 min at room temperature.The cells were then stained with 4 µL of CD206 antibody (FITC-65155, Proteintech, Hunan, China) and 5 µL of CD86 antibody (PE-65165, Proteintech, Hunan, China), followed by 40 min of incubation in the dark at 4 °C.After washing with PBS, the cells were resuspended in 500 µL of PBS.Flow cytometry analysis was performed on a NovoCyte Flow Cytometer (D1041, ACEA, Beijing, China), and data were analyzed using NovoExpress software (v.1.2.5).
Cell line and cell culture

The Ishikawa cell line was obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, VA, USA).Frozen cells were thawed in a 37 °C water bath and transferred to a centrifuge tube containing 9 mL of pre-warmed complete medium (89% DMEM, 10% FBS, 1% Pen-Strep).The cells were centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 5 min, and the supernatant was discarded.Cells were cultured at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 95% O 2 and 5% CO 2 .

For macrophage differentiation, THP-1 cells were seeded in 6-well plates at 1 × 10⁶ cells per well in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% Pen-Strep.To induce macrophage-like differentiation, 100 nM PMA (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) was added to the culture medium, and cells were incubated for 48 h.After the medium containing PMA was removed and the cells washed with PBS, they were further treated with LPS (100 ng/mL) and IFN-γ (20 ng/mL) for M1 polarization or IL-4 (20 ng/mL) and IL-13 (20 ng/mL) for M2 polarization.

A co-culture system was established using 0.4 μm pore size transwell chambers (Millipore, Merck, Germany).Ishikawa cells (5 × 10 4 ) were seeded in the lower chamber, and polarized M1 or M2 macrophages were seeded in the upper chamber at the same density (1:1 ratio).A total of 700 µL of complete medium was added to the chambers, and the cells were incubated for 24 h at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere with 95% O₂ and 5% CO₂.
Cell viability and migration assays

Cell viability was assessed using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8, C0038, Beyotime, Shanghai, China).After co-culture treatment, the medium was removed, and 10 µL of CCK-8 reagent was added to each well.Plates were incubated for 1 h at 37 °C, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (K3 PLUS, BIO-DL, Shanghai, China).Data were expressed as the mean of three independent experiments.

For the migration assay, 24-well transwell inserts were used.Inserts were pretreated with serum-free medium, PBS, and trypsin at 37 °C.Ishikawa cells in the logarithmic growth phase were harvested, resuspended in serum-free medium, and seeded in the upper chamber at a density of 5 × 10⁴ cells per well.The lower chamber was filled with 600 µL of complete medium, with or without co-cultured macrophages.After incubation for 24, 48, or 72 h, non-migrated cells were removed with cotton swabs.The inserts were then fixed with cold methanol for 20 min and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 min.Migrated cells were visualized under a light microscope, and images were captured from three different fields per well for quantification.
Statistics and visualization

The statistics for the rest of the graphs are performed using rstatix (0.7.2) and visualized using ggplot2 (3.4.3), except for the functions with the default statistics and visualization methods.To assess group differences, we used parametric tests such as Student's t-test or Welch's ANOVA when the data met the normal distribution and chi-square criteria.For non-normal data, we used non-parametric tests such as the Wilcoxon test or the Kruskal-Wallis test, followed by Tukey's post-hoc test.
Results
Identification of the patient's immunotherapy response

TIDE score was calculated for EC patients based on a standardized expression matrix, where patients with scores greater than 0 indicated immunotherapy non-response (NR), and patients with scores less than 0 indicated immunotherapy response (R) (Fig. 2A).In independent cohorts, EC patients from the R group had higher EaSIeR score compared to NR.Meanwhile, TIDE score and EaSIeR score were significantly negatively correlated in EC patients (TCGA-UCEC: P = 0.011; GSE120490: P = 0.00052) (Fig. 2B).

In addition, in the TCGA-UCEC and GSE120490 cohorts, EC patients with higher TIDE score corresponded to higher positive predictors (MHC Molecules and Effector Cells) of immunotherapy, which were significantly negatively correlated with each other and significantly positively correlated with negative predictors (Immunosuppressive Cells and Checkpoints/Immunomodulators) (Fig. 2C, D).
Patient pathological features and functional enrichment

In the TCGA-UCEC cohort, patients aged 65 years older responded well to immunotherapy.However, there were no significant differences between NR and R in terms of tumor stage, grade, and subtype (Fig. 3A).The expression of 311 genes was upregulated and 181 genes were downregulated in the R group compared to NR (Fig. 3B).Similarly, the number of genes with altered expression in the GSE120490 cohort was 56 and 86, respectively (Fig. 3C).Integrated analysis of DEGs revealed 72 common overlapping genes in the two independent cohorts (Supplemental Fig. 1A), including 38 genes with co-upregulation and 24 genes with co-downregulation, while 10 genes showed inconsistent expression trends in the two independent cohorts (Supplemental Fig. 1B).

The results of the GO enrichment analysis revealed that DEGs were predominantly associated with biological processes related to the immune, including the innate immune response and the regulation of immune response (P < 0.05).In addition, the genes were also found to be involved in cellular oncological processes such as "Cell differentiation" and "Epithelium development" (P < 0.05) (Fig. 3D).On the other hand, the KEGG enrichment analysis showed that the Toll-like receptor signaling pathway, NF-kappa B signaling pathway and cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction were up-regulated in EC patients belonging to the R group (P < 0.05).Conversely, EC patients in the NR group exhibited a preference for the WNT signaling pathway and MAPK signaling pathway (P < 0.05) (Fig. 3D).Furthermore, functional enrichment analysis of genes exhibiting consistent expression trends in two independent cohorts also indicated the aforementioned biological pathways, particularly those related to the immune (P < 0.05) (Supplemental Fig. 1C).
Differences in the tumor microenvironment

"Angiogenesis", "Tumor proliferation rate" and "protumor cytokines" were significantly enriched in EC patients from the NR group (P < 0.05) (Fig. 4A, C).In contrast, EC patients from the R group had more pronounced functional gene expression features such as "Checkpoint molecules", "Co-stimulatory receptors", and "Tumor-associated macrophages" (P < 0.05) (Fig. 4A, C).Concurrently, the gene set enrichment analysis revealed that the normalized enrichment score (NES) of "Angiogenesis" and "Tumor proliferation rate" were positive in two independent cohorts (P < 0.05) (Fig. 4B, D), thereby validating the significant activation of the current biological pathway in patients diagnosed with the NR group.Consequently, "Checkpoint molecules" and "Co-stimulatory receptors" demonstrated significant activation in the R group (P < 0.05) (Fig. 4B, D).

Based on the ESTIMATE algorithm, we determined EC patients from the R group exhibited higher immune and estimate scores, as well as lower tumor purity (Fig. 5A; Supplemental Fig. 2A).Furthermore, by TIMER and EPIC algorithms, we found that EC patients from the R group had higher infiltration of various immune cells (e.g., macrophages, neutrophils, etc.) in the TME, and significantly lower infiltration of fibroblasts and other cells than the NR group (Fig. 5B, C; Supplemental Fig. 2B, C).

The expression of immune checkpoint was upregulated in EC patients from the R group (Fig. 5D, Supplemental Fig. 2D).Chemokines, interferons, and interleukins, as well as their receptors, were highly expressed in EC patients from the R group (Fig. 5D, Supplemental Fig. 2D).
Comprehensive genomic variant analysis between NR and R

The top 20 genes, including RPRD1B, exhibited a stronger inclination towards mutation in NR compared to R, whereby there was up to a 7-fold difference in mutation frequency for the same gene (Fig. 5A).Moreover, missense mutations prevailed among these genes.RPRD1B, in particular, remained unaltered in R and had a mutation frequency of 6% in NR.In addition, NR exhibited a mutation rate of 32% for CTNNB1, which was double in R. Notably, the zinc finger gene family (such as ZNF627, ZNF28C, ZNF217, and ZNF570) had a significantly higher mutation frequency in NR (Fig. 6A).

Our analysis revealed that mutations in NR were enriched in DNA mismatch repair features (COSMIC Signature 6 and COSMIC Signature 26), whereas mutations in R were associated with APEOC enzymes and 5-methylcytosine.Furthermore, the POLE polymerase feature (COSMIC Signature 10) was detected in both NR and R (Fig. 6B, C).The mode of somatic mutation action was mainly defined by co-occurrence, with more extensive interactions illustrated between mutations in NR.It is noteworthy that some gene sets, such as CTNNB1 and LIG4, RPRD1B and HELZ, were exclusively present in NR (Fig. 6D, E).Furthermore, the results of the enrichment analysis demonstrated that the top 20 genes were closely associated with biological pathways such as "Positive regulation of myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity", "Chromosome organization" and "Macromolecule biosynthetic process", and were significantly enriched in immunerelated pathways such as "Leukocyte transendothelial migration", "Neutrophil extracellular trap formation" and "Primary immunodeficiency" (P < 0.05) (Supplemental Fig. 3A).On the basis of these findings, it can be hypothesized that the substantial immune infiltration observed in the R group may be influenced by mutations in these genes.

For CNV, EC patients had higher variant scores in R (Fig. 7A).The amplification frequencies of the top 5 sites in NR and R are identical, namely 1q22, 1q21.3,1q32.1, 1q25.3 and 1q42.3,listed in order.R demonstrates a higher frequency of variation than NR for the same amplification site, as exemplified by 1q22.Furthermore, among the top 20 sites with the highest frequency of variation, there are three distinct deletion sites (16q23.1,19q13.3 and 16q21) in R, all possessing a higher frequency of variation compared to 16q23.1 (30%) in NR (Fig. 7B, C).
Single-cell analyses reveal a key cell population for immunotherapy response

After undergoing quality control and filtering, a total of 47,264 cells met the pretreatment threshold and were included in the subsequent analysis.Following the application of dimensionality reduction, batch correction, and unsupervised cell clustering, all the cells were classified into 7 distinct clusters, which were also presented as UMAP plots (Fig. 8A).The UMAP plots demonstrated that cells from different patients within the same cluster overlapped with each other, and the effect of the source difference on cell clustering was effectively corrected (Fig. 8B).

We mapped the cell markers based on their expression levels and found that each cell cluster showed a distinct high expression of a particular cell marker.Specifically, cluster 0 was associated with lymphocytes, cluster 1 with unciliated epithelium, cluster 2 with fibroblasts, cluster 3 with ciliated epithelium, cluster 4 with smooth muscle cells, cluster 5 with endotheliocytes, cluster 6 with TAMs (Fig. 8C).In addition, we verified the correspondence between the cell clusters and cell types based on the signature genes identified by Ren et al. [34] (Fig. 9A).Finally, we identified and renamed the above seven cell populations (Fig. 9B).

The proportion of various cell types differed significantly among the patients.Patient "EC4" had more than 50% lymphocytes, patient "EC1" had the highest proportion of smooth muscle cells, and patient "EC2" had the highest proportion of macrophages (Fig. 9C).

Based on the results of the Scissor algorithm, we have discovered that in the TCGA-UCEC and GSE120490 cohorts, there were significantly more TAMs linked to immunotherapy response.However, we observed that the other types of cells did not show Fig. 7 Copy number variation profiles of EC patients in the TCGA-UCEC cohort.A GISTIC score of EC patients.Red indicates amplification (Amp).Blue indicates deletion (Del).B Oncoplot of the top 20 most frequently genes with CNV in NR.C Oncoplot of the top 20 most frequently genes with CNV in R consistency in the results, which suggests that TAMs might be the key cell population that influence immunotherapy response in EC patients (Fig. 9D, E).
Investigating the link between M1-and M2-like TAMs and immunotherapy response

In order to investigate how TAMs impact the immunotherapy response in EC patients, we isolated TAMs and reanalyzed in a simplified way, which gave us three new cell clusters (Fig. 10A).We then identified the top 15 genes that were unique to the each.We found that cluster 1 had significantly higher expression of M1-like TAMs activation-related genes such as CD86, CXCL9, CXCL10 and S100A9.In contrast, cluster 0 displayed a significant up-regulation of M2-like TAMs, inducing genes such as SPP1, CD206, CCL2 and CCL7.Cluster 2 did not show any immune/inflammation-related features, but instead had higher expression of cell proliferation-associated genes such as TOP2A and MK167 (Fig. 10B).

According to the GSEA analysis, we observed significant upregulation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway and cGMP-PKG signaling pathway in cluster 0, which are associated with anti-inflammatory and pro-tumor effects.On the other hand, we found that cluster 1 exhibited significant activation of antigen processing and presentation, as well as cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction (Fig. 10C).Additionally, we noticed that cell cycle features (S.score and G2M.score) were mainly concentrated in cluster 2, while pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory features were enriched in clusters 0 and 1, respectively (Fig. 10D).As a result, we defined three distinct cell clusters as M1-like TAMs, M2-like TAMs and prolif-TAMs, respectively.

Further mapping Scissor's results, we found that M1-like TAMs occupied the highest proportion of TAMs associated with immunotherapy response in EC patients, and TAMs associated with immune non-response in EC patients were predominantly M2-like TAMs (Fig. 11A, B).In addition, we included the Scissor results from two cohorts (TCGA-UCEC and GSE120490).We retained all the cells that were identified as both R or NR simultaneously for cell-cell interaction analysis (Fig. 11C).The study revealed that M2-like TAMs were the primary senders and receivers in the communication network of the NR group (Fig. 11D).They communicated more frequently with non-immune cells, such as endothelial and epithelial cells.Abundant ligand-receptor pairs were observed between these cells, promoting angiogenesis and cell proliferation, including VEGFB-VEGFR1, SPP1-(ITGA5 + ITGB1), HBEGF-EGFR and so on (Supplemental Fig. 3C).In contrast, M1-like TAMs accounted for the highest proportion of the communication network in the R group (Fig. 11D).However, they mainly communicated with immune cells, involving multiple immune activators such as CD86, CXCL10 and HMGB1 (Supplemental Fig. 3D).
Responders to immunotherapy exhibited significantly increased infiltration of M1-like TAMs in EC patients

To validate the impact of TAMs on the immunotherapeutic efficacy in EC patients, immunohistochemistry (IHC) and flow cytometry analysis was performed on postoperative tumor tissues and peripheral blood samples from patients who underwent neoadjuvant immunotherapy.Patients were divided into two groups: non-response (NR) and response (R) based on their postoperative pathological response.As shown in Fig. 12A, IHC staining revealed significantly higher the staining scores for CD86 (M1-like TAMs marker) and lower the staining scores for CD206 (M2-like TAMs marker) in the tumor tissues of R compared to NR (all P < 0.001) (Fig. 12A).

The results of the subsequent flow cytometry analysis further corroborated these findings.As shown in Fig. 12B, a higher percentage of M1-like TAMs (CD86+) was observed in the NR group of patients compared to NR, with 72.35% of PBMCs from the R group compared to 18.18% in the NR group (all P < 0.001).Conversely, the proportion of M2-like TAMs (CD206+) was found to be significantly higher in the NR group, where 86.03% of PBMCs were CD206 + compared to only 18.27% in the R group (P < 0.001).The findings of this study indicate that an increased presence of M1-like TAMs and a decreased presence of M2-like TAMs within the tumor microenvironment are associated with a more favorable therapeutic response to immunotherapy in EC patients.
M1-like TAMs inhibited Ishikawa cells proliferation and migration

The investigation was conducted with the objective of ascertaining the impact of TAMs phenotypes on the proliferation and migration of Ishikawa cells.To this end, a coculture system was established (Fig. 12C), and CCK-8 and migration assays were performed.The results demonstrated that the proliferation of Ishikawa cells co-cultured with M1-like TAMs was notably inhibited compared to those cultured alone or with M2-like TAMs at various time points (24, 48 and 72 h) (all P < 0.05) (Fig. 12D).Specifically, the cell viability in the Ishikawa + M1 group decreased progressively over time, with the most pronounced inhibition observed at 72 h (Fig. 12D).Furthermore, migration assays further revealed significant differences in cell migration ability.After 24, 48, and 72 h of co-culture, Ishikawa cells co-cultured with M1-like TAMs exhibited a marked decrease in the number of migrated cells compared to the Ishikawa and the Ishikawa + M2 group (all P < 0.05) (Fig. 12E).Interestingly, migration was less inhibited in the Ishikawa + M2 group, showing higher migratory activity at all time points compared to the Ishikawa + M1 group, especially at 72 h (all P < 0.01) (Fig. 12E).This finding suggests that M1-like TAMs strongly suppress the proliferative and migratory capacities of Ishikawa cells, whereas the M2-like TAMs appear to promote migration and cell viability over time.
Discussion

In recent years, the field of immunotherapy has markedly revolutionized the management of various malignancies [7-9, 11, 13, 14].Unlike traditional chemotherapy or radiotherapy, immunotherapy offers prolonged response durations and sustained survival benefits [11,13,14].A comprehensive analysis involving 1,861 patients diagnosed with melanoma revealed that immunotherapy interventions resulted in a five-year survival rate of 20-26%, significantly exceeding the 10% survival rate associated with conventional treatment modalities.Notably, the survival rate remained stable between the five-and ten-year intervals, underscoring the enduring effectiveness of this treatment modality [60].Nonetheless, it is important to acknowledge that the response to immunotherapy differs across various malignancies, with some patients exhibiting limited sensitivity, leading to objective remission rates below 50%.A recent study by Margul et al. [61] reported that objective remission rates for patients with endometrial cancer (EC) in phase Ib/II clinical trials of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) were as low as 13%.Combination immunotherapy treatments typically result in more favorable clinical outcomes than monotherapies; however, they are also associated with an increased risk of severe adverse effects [62].The efficacy of immunotherapy is modulated by various factors, including the tumor microenvironment (TME), mutational burden, mismatch repair defects, and specific methylation patterns [63].Predicting treatment outcomes in EC patients cannot be reliably achieved through the consideration of a single factor.Given the complexity of this issue, a comprehensive analysis is essential for investigating the effectiveness of immunotherapy in EC.Present trials [64][65][66] frequently encounter limitations due to insufficient comprehensive data, as they predominantly focus on pretreatment gene expression profiles.To overcome these constraints, our study utilizes the TCGA-UCEC dataset, which includes multi-omics data.We employ the TIDE computational framework to predict immunotherapy responses by evaluating tumor immune dysfunction and exclusion scores in EC patients.Jiang et al. [37] identified that TIDE exhibited superior predictive capability relative to other biomarkers for assessing immunotherapy response.To reduce the likelihood of false positives, we performed further validation of our results employing the EaSIeR and ImmunoPhenoScore algorithms, with the GSE120490 dataset serving as a reference.This rigorous methodology produced consistent outcomes across multiple independent datasets.

In 2013, the Cancer Genome Atlas [67] delineated endometrial cancer (EC) into four distinct subtypes: copy number high (CN-high), copy number low (CN-low), mismatch repair deficient (MSI), and polymerase ε mutant (POLE).Notably, the MSI subtype has been recognized for its potential responsiveness to immunotherapy, attributed to increased immune infiltration within the TME.Our study's findings demonstrate a uniform distribution of these subtypes between NR and R to treatment.Importantly, patients aged 65 and older showed a higher response rate to immunotherapy, aligning with previous research that identifies age as a significant factor influencing immune efficacy [68].Moreover, our observations indicated that the NR demonstrated increased levels of cell differentiation, angiogenesis, and tumor proliferation characteristics, coupled with higher tumor purity and reduced expression of immune checkpoint markers.Conversely, the R showed a more pronounced association with immune-related factors, as supported by pathway enrichment analysis and the composition of the TME.During the progression of endometrial cancer (EC), the unchecked proliferation of tumor cells necessitates a continuous supply of nutrients, thus promoting angiogenesis within the TME and facilitating metastasis [69,70].Consequently, angiogenesis is recognized as a negative prognostic factor in endometrial cancer (EC).The mechanisms of cell proliferation and angiogenesis involve a variety of stromal cells, including cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), endothelial cells, and mesenchymal stem cells.For example, endothelial cells release vascular factors that facilitate cancer progression, while CAFs play a role in angiogenesis and the remodeling of the stromal environment [71].Alexander et al. [46] observed that patients exhibiting predominant angiogenesis and stromal remodeling demonstrated a reduced response rate to immunotherapy.In contrast, patients exhibiting a high infiltration of T and B lymphocytes within the TME, alongside the expression of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules and antitumor cytokines, showed enhanced survival rates and heightened sensitivity to immunotherapy.These findings underscore the critical influence of TME composition on the immunotherapeutic response in EC patients, thereby indicating the potential for optimizing therapeutic efficacy.

RPRD1B, alternatively referred to as CREPT, possesses a C-terminal domain interacting domain (CID) that facilitates its interaction with the C-terminal domain (CTD) of the largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII).Research by Lu et al. [72] has shown a marked upregulation of RPRD1B expression in tumor tissues relative to matched normal tissues across eight solid tumor types, including endometrial cancer (EC).Subsequent studies have substantiated these observations, indicating that RPRD1B is instrumental in enhancing cell proliferation, migration, and invasion [73].Furthermore, the suppression of RPRD1B via knockdown methodologies has been demonstrated to significantly hinder tumor progression [73].Patients with heightened RPRD1B expression levels have also been correlated with an unfavorable prognosis [74,75].In addition, a study by Zhang et al. [76] employing data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), found that nearly 50% of colorectal cancer patients displayed copy number alterations of RPRD1B, leading to its overexpression.In this study, patients classified within the non-responder (NR) cohort, who did not exhibit a favorable response to immunotherapy, demonstrated a higher incidence of RPRD1B deletions.In contrast, individuals in the R group did not present with these genetic alterations.Furthermore, the NR group showed a significant elevation in tumor progression indicators, including cell proliferation and angiogenesis, potentially attributable to the presence of RPRD1B mutations.Notably, CTNNB1 mutations, which rank among the most prevalent WNT-activating mutations in endometrial cancer (EC), possess the capacity to produce stable β-catenin proteins, thereby facilitating enhanced cell proliferation [77,78].These mutations are significantly correlated with an unfavorable prognosis in patients [79].A study by Elena et al. [80] revealed that individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer who exhibited resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) demonstrated a higher incidence of CTNNB1 mutations.Additionally, it was observed that patients harboring CTNNB1 mutations showed markedly decreased T-cell infiltration within the TME, indicative of a cold immune phenotype.These findings are consistent with the present study's observations of increased CTNNB1 mutation rates and reduced immune infiltration in the NR group, suggesting that CTNNB1 mutations may contribute to immunotherapy resistance by altering the TME.Zinc finger proteins (ZNPs) represent the most abundant family of transcription factors in the human genome.Research [81] has demonstrated that these proteins promote a range of biological processes, including cell proliferation, metastasis, and drug resistance, in various tumor types.In a recent study, Mu et al. [82] found that IKZF1, a member of the zinc finger protein family, enhances PD-L1 expression and activates immune-related signaling pathways in osteosarcoma cells, thereby improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint therapy.Additionally, current studies indicate that the mutation frequency in ZNPs is significantly higher in the NR group compared to the R group.Consequently, we hypothesize that the elevated mutation burden of ZNPs in the NR group may disrupt analogous regulatory mechanisms, such as the IKZF1-PD-L1 axis, thereby fostering the development of an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and diminishing responsiveness to immunotherapy.Similarly, genomic alterations such as mutations in CTNNB1 and RPRD1B may impede the efficacy of immunotherapy in patients with EC by facilitating tumor progression and altering the TME.

Recent advancements in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) have significantly enhanced our comprehension of the TME at a cellular level.In contrast to bulk RNA sequencing, scRNA-seq provides a detailed understanding of cellular subpopulations and gene expression patterns.In our study, the Scissor algorithm was utilized to highlight the critical role of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) within the TME of EC patients, emphasizing their influence on individual responses to immunotherapy.Analysis of the subpopulations revealed that the proportion of M1-like TAMs in the responder group was markedly higher than that of M2-like TAMs or proliferative TAMs.M1-like TAMs are actively involved in the immunotherapeutic response within tissues, primarily responsible for the removal of damaged tissue and tumor cells.In contrast, M2-like TAMs are associated with angiogenesis and tissue repair, thereby actively promoting cancer progression [83][84][85][86].Numerous preclinical and clinical studies have supported the prevailing view that TAMs predominantly exhibit an M2-like phenotype and demonstrate significant infiltration within the TME, thus representing a significant risk factor for cancer progression [86,87].Recent studies have demonstrated that the transformation of M2-like TAMs into M1-like TAMs enhances macrophage-mediated anti-tumor activity and effectively hinders tumor progression [88,89].In murine tumor models, the application of M1-like TAMs activators has been observed to substantially increase the M1/M2 ratio, thereby synergistically amplifying the anti-tumor efficacy of immunotherapeutic interventions [90][91][92].From a mechanistic perspective, M1-like TAMs not only engage in direct phagocytosis but also enhance cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) activity through the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-12, among others.They also improve antigen presentation and activate additional pathways, collectively exerting an inhibitory effect on tumor growth.In contrast, M2-like TAMs release Th2-type cytokines that facilitate tumor proliferation and actively recruit immunosuppressive cells, thereby hindering the anti-tumor response of T cells [83][84][85][86].Additionally, our investigation into cellular communication identified a substantial exchange of signaling molecules between M1-like TAMs and other immune cells within the TME of patients from the R group.This exchange involves a diverse array of ligand-receptor interactions, including CD86-CD28 [93], CXCL10-CXCR3 [94], HMGB1-RAGE [95] among others, which have been shown to play active roles in immune activation and tumor eradication.In contrast, M2-like TAMs within the TME of patients in the NR group seem to promote tumor progression by conveying angiogenic and cell proliferation signals to endothelial or epithelial cells through cytokines such as SPP1, VEGFB, and HBEGF [96][97][98][99].Overall, the findings of this study suggest that TAM subpopulations play a pivotal role in the immunotherapy response of EC patients.The presence of M1-like TAMs within the TME of individuals in the R group appears to have enhanced the immunotherapy response, leading to tumor eradication.Conversely, the presence of M2-like TAMs in the NR group appears to facilitate tumor progression by promoting angiogenesis and hindering the recruitment of immune cells.This differentiation highlights the potential of targeted TAM manipulation as a strategy for modulating the TME in the treatment of EC patients.

Despite the significant findings of our study regarding immunotherapy responses in EC patients, it is crucial to recognize the limitations inherent in our research.Firstly, the utilization of publicly accessible datasets, although convenient, may introduce confounding variables, including variability in data collection methodologies and patient selection criteria, which can limit the generalizability of our findings.The retrospective design of the study further introduces potential selection bias, as these datasets may not comprehensively represent the broader EC population.Additionally, while advanced computational tools such as TIDE, EaSIeR, and ImmunoPhenoScore were employed, their predictive accuracy is restricted by inherent model assumptions and the complex nature of the TME.Furthermore, the dependence on bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing techniques may introduce measurement bias, as these methodologies may not fully capture the heterogeneity of immune interactions in EC.To address these limitations and enhance the clinical relevance of our findings, future research should incorporate prospective, multi-institutional cohort studies aimed at providing a more comprehensive understanding of the molecular landscape of EC.
Conclusion

In conclusion, this comprehensive study elucidates the complex interplay between immunotherapy, genomic variations, and tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).Our findings reveal the variability in the efficacy of immunotherapy among patients with endometrial cancer (EC), which is modulated by a diverse array of factors, including patient age, tumor microenvironment (TME) composition, and specific genetic alterations.Therefore, this research not only advances the understanding of the fundamental biological mechanisms underlying EC development and treatment response but also highlights the potential for personalized medical interventions to optimize EC therapy.By identifying and targeting specific subpopulations of TAMs and understanding patient-specific genetic profiles, there is a significant opportunity to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy.This advancement could lead to the development of more effective and personalized treatment strategies for EC patients.
